title: What you actually download when you download a model
why: You have run local models already. Understanding the package lets you tell which change could alter its behavior. A model is a numerical function; a runtime is the program that executes it.
how: A checkpoint stores learned weights. Configuration describes how those numbers connect. A tokenizer maps text to token IDs; a chat template adds role and turn markers. MLX is an array-computation framework; MLX LM adds language-model loading, generation and adaptation. These pieces work together, but changing the runtime does not itself teach the weights anything.
formula: output = decode(model(encode(formatted conversation))). Read this inside out: format messages, encode text as IDs, compute scores with weights, choose IDs, decode them as text. Application validation comes afterward.
example: For a NoteEchoes-style reminder, the model proposes text describing the action. Your application parses and checks it before creating a reminder. Downloading a different tokenizer can change the IDs even when the visible request stays the same.
experiment: Inspect one existing model folder. Record the weight files, config, tokenizer, template, model revision and runtime version. Do not download another model for this exercise.
question: If your model generates text, has it automatically gained permission to create reminders?
answer: No. Generation produces data. Application code and operating-system permission determine which actions can execute.

title: Parameters, tensors and the memory budget
why: A model name such as 7B tells you how many learned numbers it contains, not how much total RAM a running application will consume.
how: A tensor is an array with a shape and a numeric representation. Parameter count counts stored learned values. Bit width measures storage per value. Eight bits make one byte, so multiplying parameters by bits and dividing by eight gives ideal weight bytes. Runtime memory also includes cache, intermediate results and overhead.
formula: weight bytes ≈ P × b / 8; total live memory ≈ weights + KV cache + activations + runtime overhead. P is parameter count and b is average stored bits per parameter. GB here means 1,000,000,000 bytes; GiB means 1,073,741,824 bytes.
example: For an illustrative 1-billion-parameter model, ideal weights need 2 GB at 16 bits, 1 GB at 8 bits, or 0.5 GB at 4 bits. Real files include metadata and may leave some layers at higher precision.
experiment: Estimate the three sizes for your model, then compare with actual file size. List possible reasons for the difference before measuring process memory.
question: Does a 4 GB model file guarantee it can run in 4 GB of free RAM?
answer: No. File size is only part of the live memory budget, and context and temporary allocations can increase the peak.

title: Storage precision is different from sampling temperature
why: Both quantization and temperature can change the words you see. They act at different stages, so confusing them makes experiments hard to interpret.
how: Quantization changes the representation of weights used to compute scores. Temperature changes how existing scores become a sampling distribution. Greedy selection chooses the largest score directly. A sampled token probability is not a calibrated probability that an action is correct.
formula: p_i = exp(z_i/T) / sum_j exp(z_j/T), for T > 0. z_i is the score for token i. Dividing by a smaller positive T increases score differences before normalization; the weights themselves remain unchanged.
example: Two next-token scores 2 and 1 produce probabilities about 0.73 and 0.27 at T=1; at T=0.5 they become about 0.88 and 0.12. A 4-bit conversion may change the scores before either calculation.
experiment: Compare two temperatures on one fixed model. Then compare 8-bit and 4-bit with the same prompt and greedy decoding. Record these as two separate experiments.
question: Does lowering temperature recover information lost during weight quantization?
answer: No. It changes token selection from the scores available; it does not restore the original weights.

title: What 4-bit and 8-bit quantization really mean
why: Quantization lets you store weights with fewer bits. To understand its tradeoff, follow one weight through compression and reconstruction.
how: In a simple uniform scheme, choose a minimum a and maximum c, divide that interval into representable levels, and store the nearest level index. With b bits there are 2^b possible indices. Reconstruction maps the index back to an approximate weight. This is a teaching scheme; real formats may use groups, nonuniform levels or different scaling conventions.
formula: s = (c − a)/(2^b − 1); q = clip(round((w − a)/s), 0, 2^b − 1); reconstructed w = a + s q. Here s is level spacing, w the original weight, and q the stored integer index. Without clipping, rounding error is at most s/2.
example: On [−1,1], 4-bit has 16 levels and s=2/15≈0.1333. Weight 0.30 becomes index 10 and reconstructs as 0.3333. With 8-bit, s=2/255≈0.00784; index 166 reconstructs as 0.30196. More levels reduce this particular rounding error.
experiment: Calculate both reconstructions for −0.42. Explain why a smaller weight error does not automatically imply a proportionate improvement in application accuracy.
question: Does 4-bit mean a model has only four possible weights?
answer: No. Four bits encode 16 indices per quantization group; group scales and offsets map those indices to reconstructed values.

title: Group size, scales and quantization overhead
why: A single unusually large weight can force a coarse scale for many small weights. Grouping lets different portions of a matrix use different ranges.
how: A group is a set of weights sharing quantization metadata. Smaller groups can fit local ranges more closely, but need more metadata. Storage precision and computation precision are separate: packed weights can be reconstructed and used in higher-precision arithmetic. A label such as 4-bit does not specify the whole format.
formula: ideal storage bits ≈ P b + ceil(P/g) m. P is weight count, b bits per packed weight, g weights per group, and m metadata bits per group. This estimate ignores padding and unquantized tensors.
example: For 1,024 weights at 4 bits with a 16-bit scale and a 16-bit offset per group, g=64 needs 512+64=576 bytes. At g=32 it needs 512+128=640 bytes. The second layout spends more space on local scales.
experiment: Read your converted model's quantization configuration: bits, group size, mode and any layer exceptions. Compare two versions only after recording all four.
question: Are two models labeled 4-bit necessarily numerically identical?
answer: No. Group size, scaling method, calibration, original checkpoint and layer choices can all differ.

title: What changes when you fine-tune a local model
why: Inference uses learned weights to make a prediction. Fine-tuning uses examples and an error signal to change selected learned values. This connects your local projects to today's gradient lesson.
how: Run a forward pass, compare the prediction with the desired target, differentiate that loss with respect to trainable parameters, then apply an optimizer update. A frozen parameter still participates in prediction but receives no update. Changing temperature is inference configuration; it is not fine-tuning.
formula: For plain gradient descent: w_new = w_old − η × ∂L/∂w. η is the chosen learning rate; the derivative tells how loss changes locally as w changes. Real optimizers such as Adam also use accumulated state, so this is the simplest update rule, not their complete formula.
example: With prediction 2w, target 6 and loss (2w−6)^2, the gradient is 4(2w−6). At w=1 it is −16. With η=0.1 the update is +1.6, so w becomes 2.6 and loss falls from 16 to 0.64. A NoteEchoes adapter applies the same principle to many trainable values and language-model loss.
experiment: For one of your fine-tuning configurations, identify what is trainable, what is frozen, which loss is minimized and which optimizer is used. Explain each before running training.
question: Does a negative gradient mean the weight should decrease?
answer: For a positive learning rate in gradient descent, subtracting a negative gradient increases the weight. The gradient describes the uphill direction.

title: Fine-tuning examples, targets and validation splits
why: A training run can learn formatting mistakes or memorize examples. Good data defines the behavior you want and gives you an honest way to check improvement.
how: Supervised language-model fine-tuning predicts target tokens from preceding tokens. A loss mask selects which positions contribute to the objective; assistant-only loss focuses on response tokens. Train examples drive updates, validation selects settings, and a held-out test set assesses the final choice. Near-duplicate conversations crossing splits can overstate generalization.
formula: L = −(1/N) sum_t m_t log p(target_t | earlier tokens), where m_t is 1 for a scored target position and 0 otherwise, and N=sum_t m_t. The minus sign turns low target probability into a large penalty.
example: For a reminder project, pair a user request with the desired structured proposal. If 'remind me tomorrow' appears in training and almost the same wording appears in testing, passing it gives weak evidence for unseen phrasing.
experiment: Inspect ten of your training conversations after template formatting. Mark the target tokens. Split by source or conversation family where appropriate, then look for duplicates across splits.
question: Can a falling training loss establish that unseen requests improved?
answer: No. Check held-out examples, including ambiguous requests and failure cases, with application-level metrics.

title: MLX lazy evaluation and automatic differentiation
why: MLX code can describe calculations before executing them. This affects both how gradients are produced and how you time a computation.
how: Lazy operations build a dependency graph. Evaluation materializes needed results. Automatic differentiation follows the computation to calculate derivatives; it does not select your learning rate or decide whether your data is good. MLX exposes function transformations such as grad and explicit evaluation through eval.
formula: If f(w)=(2w−6)^2, grad(f)(w)=4(2w−6). This is the chain rule applied by software: outer square contributes 2(2w−6), inner expression contributes 2. Evaluating f and its gradient produces numbers for a particular w.
example: On a supported MLX installation, define f=lambda w:(2*w-6)**2, set w=mx.array(1.0), and compute g=mx.grad(f)(w). After mx.eval(g), g.item() is −16. This is a tiny numeric check, not a model training run.
experiment: Run that calculation in your existing MLX environment with import mlx.core as mx. When benchmarking larger operations, include evaluation inside the measured region, warm up first, and ensure the relevant work completes.
question: Why can timing only the creation of a lazy expression look unrealistically fast?
answer: It may mostly time graph construction while the actual numerical work happens later when a result is evaluated.

title: Apple Silicon unified memory and device execution
why: A local model must fit alongside your other applications. Shared physical memory reduces some transfers, but it does not remove the need to budget allocations.
how: MLX arrays can be used by its CPU and GPU execution paths on Apple Silicon within unified memory. Computation still requires scheduling and synchronization. Unified memory does not mean every operation is free of temporary copies, nor does it mean MLX automatically executes on the Apple Neural Engine. Hardware support depends on the runtime and operation.
formula: available budget = physical memory − operating-system use − other applications − safety headroom. This is a planning estimate; actual peak memory must be measured during your workload.
example: On an illustrative 16 GB machine, reserving 6 GB for the system, other apps and headroom leaves about 10 GB for the experiment. A 7B model's ideal 4-bit weights are 3.5 GB, but cache and temporary allocations still consume the remainder.
experiment: Record idle memory and peak memory for one existing model at two context lengths. Keep other applications and model settings stable. Compare results with your weight-only estimate from Day 2.
question: Does shared CPU/GPU memory make a 16 GB Mac equivalent to a machine with unlimited model memory?
answer: No. CPU, GPU, applications and caches compete for the same finite physical capacity.

title: Read the model configuration before guessing its shape
why: A model's parameter count does not tell you its layer count, hidden width or number of cache heads. Those determine different costs.
how: Hidden width is the length of each token representation. Layers repeat transformations. Attention query heads ask for information; key/value heads supply cached information. Grouped-query attention shares fewer key/value heads among more query heads. Exact dimensions belong to the checkpoint configuration, not to a generic family name.
formula: A dense matrix with O output coordinates and I input coordinates has O×I weights, plus O biases if present. For standard attention, query projection width is H_q×d and key/value projection width is H_kv×d; H denotes head count and d head width.
example: An illustrative layer with I=1,024, H_q=16 and d=64 has 1,048,576 query-projection weights. If H_kv=4, its key projection has 262,144 weights. Fewer KV heads also reduce cache storage.
experiment: Read your config and record hidden size, layers, query heads, KV heads and head dimension. Distinguish explicitly stored fields from values you derive under an architectural assumption.
question: Should you always use query-head count in a KV-cache memory calculation?
answer: No. Use the number of key/value heads; in grouped-query attention it is smaller than query-head count.

title: KV cache: why long conversations consume more memory
why: During generation, the model repeatedly consults earlier tokens. Caching their keys and values avoids recomputing them, but memory grows with the stored context.
how: Each attention layer saves a key vector and a value vector for each cached token and KV head. These are computed activations, separate from learned weights. Quantizing weights to 4 bits does not automatically quantize the cache to 4 bits.
formula: KV bytes ≈ 2×L×B×T×H_kv×d×s. The 2 counts keys and values; L is layers, B batch size, T cached tokens, H_kv KV heads, d head width, and s bytes per cache number. This assumes a full dense cache without sliding windows, packing overhead or sharing.
example: For L=16, B=1, T=2,048, H_kv=4, d=64 and s=2, cache size is 33,554,432 bytes, or 32 MiB. Doubling T doubles this estimate, although total process memory need not double.
experiment: Calculate your model's expected cache growth per additional 1,000 tokens. Compare two runs with fixed output length and different prompt lengths.
question: Why can a small quantized model still run out of memory on a long prompt?
answer: Its weights may fit while the growing cache and temporary activations exceed remaining memory.

title: Prefill, decode and useful latency measurements
why: The delay before the first token and the speed of later tokens feel different to the user. One tokens-per-second number can hide that distinction.
how: Prefill processes the prompt and prepares its cached representations. Decode produces successive output tokens, reusing the cache. Loading the model is another cost. Small-batch decode can be limited by moving weights through memory; prompt processing may use parallel computation more effectively. Neither bottleneck is universal.
formula: total time ≈ load time + time to first token + (N−1)×mean later-token time, for N emitted tokens, with time to first token measured after loading. The definition of each timing boundary must stay consistent.
example: After a model is loaded, first token at 0.4 s plus 19 more tokens at 0.05 s each gives 1.35 s for 20 tokens. Reporting only 20 tokens/s hides the initial wait. These are illustrative numbers, not NoteEchoes measurements.
experiment: Measure a short and a long prompt with the same model and output budget. Record cold load separately from warmed prefill and decode.
question: Will halving weight storage necessarily double generation speed?
answer: No. Kernels, reconstruction work, cache traffic and other bottlenecks can change the result. Measure on your hardware.

title: Chat templates, special tokens and structured output
why: A fine-tuned model learned from a particular input format. A template mismatch can look like a weak model or a failed quantization even when neither is the cause.
how: A chat template converts role-labeled messages into the exact text and special-token structure expected by the model. Tokenization then turns it into IDs. Stop tokens indicate completion. JSON instructions influence generation; a parser checks syntax and a schema checks required fields and types. Valid JSON alone does not establish a correct action.
formula: messages → chat template → token IDs → model scores → generated IDs → decoded text → parse → schema and semantic checks. Each arrow has its own possible failure.
example: If your adapter saw assistant-start markers during training but inference omits them, it may continue the user text instead of answering. A proposal with valid JSON but tomorrow's wrong date is still an application failure.
experiment: Compare the rendered training prompt and inference prompt for one identical conversation. Check role markers, stop IDs, added system text and whether a generation prompt is expected.
question: If a 4-bit model emits invalid JSON, what should you check before blaming bit width?
answer: Check the same input/template, tokenizer, stop settings and output limit, then compare against the unconverted baseline on the same cases.

title: Choose prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning by the failure
why: You have several ways to improve a local application. Each changes a different part of the system and solves a different kind of problem.
how: Prompting supplies instructions at inference. Retrieval supplies selected external information. Fine-tuning changes learned behavior through weight updates. New personal notes usually belong in a searchable store; a consistent output format may benefit from supervised examples. None of these makes application validation unnecessary.
formula: prediction = f_weights(instructions, retrieved evidence, request). Prompting changes instructions, retrieval changes evidence, and fine-tuning changes weights. This expression is a dependency map rather than an arithmetic formula.
example: If NoteEchoes cannot find yesterday's note, updating its adapter is an indirect way to repair a missing retrieval result. If it finds the correct note but repeatedly produces the wrong field names, examine instructions, constraints or fine-tuning.
experiment: Sort ten real failures into missing knowledge, wrong behavior, inference configuration or application bug. Choose one intervention per group and state what would count as improvement.
question: Does fine-tuning on today's notes keep the model automatically synchronized with notes added tomorrow?
answer: No. Training updates a particular snapshot. Retrieval can fetch newly indexed information without repeating that training.

title: Local embeddings: index memory and compatibility
why: A local retrieval system often needs an embedding model in addition to a generator. Its vectors and index consume memory and must remain compatible.
how: An embedding maps text to a numeric vector for similarity search. Documents and queries must use compatible encoders and preprocessing. Changing the embedding model can change the coordinate system, so old document vectors often need recomputing. Generator quantization and embedding precision are separate settings.
formula: raw vector bytes = N×D×s. N is number of document vectors, D their dimension, and s bytes per stored coordinate. This excludes index structures, document text and embedding-model weights.
example: 10,000 note chunks with 384 float32 coordinates each require 10,000×384×4=15,360,000 bytes, about 15.36 MB before index overhead. Halving storage bytes per coordinate halves this component, but similarity quality needs checking.
experiment: Record your encoder, vector dimension, normalization rule, chunking method and index format. Retrieve a fixed set of questions before and after any index change.
question: Can you swap the query embedding model while keeping unrelated old document vectors?
answer: Their coordinates may no longer mean the same things. Rebuild or explicitly verify compatibility instead of assuming equal dimensions are sufficient.

title: Build a fair 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit comparison
why: A convincing comparison isolates precision. Otherwise a different prompt, model revision or generation limit may explain the outcome.
how: Start from the same source checkpoint and keep tokenizer, template, task set and decoding settings fixed. Record quantization method and group size. Compare task quality, memory, first-token delay and generation speed. A smaller file can be useful even when speed barely changes, provided quality remains acceptable.
formula: quality difference = converted pass rate − baseline pass rate. Memory saving fraction = 1 − converted peak memory / baseline peak memory. Compute both on matching workloads; distinguish total process memory from weight-file storage.
example: In an illustrative 100-case test, baseline passes 94, 8-bit passes 94 and 4-bit passes 91. Inspect which three cases changed; three date-extraction errors may matter more than three harmless wording differences.
experiment: Prepare a comparison table for your existing versions. Fill unknown measurements with 'not measured', not estimates. Include model revision, bits, groups, prompt settings, pass count, peak memory and timing.
question: Can a single pleasant answer prove the 4-bit version matches the baseline?
answer: No. Use a fixed representative set and examine regressions by failure type, ideally with repeated timing runs.

title: Full fine-tuning versus LoRA
why: Updating every weight can require substantial memory. LoRA restricts the trainable change to a smaller factorized matrix while retaining the base model.
how: For a linear layer, full fine-tuning learns changes to every element of W. LoRA freezes W and learns two smaller matrices whose product adds an adjustment. Rank r limits the factorization size. It is capacity you choose, not a direct quality score.
formula: y=(W+sBA)x. W has shape [O,I], A [r,I], B [O,r]; s is an adapter scaling factor. Full weight count is OI; LoRA adds rI+Or=r(I+O) trainable values. The factorization is why fewer values can express a structured update.
example: For I=O=1,024 and r=8, full W has 1,048,576 values; A and B together have 16,384, or 1/64 as many. Across a whole model, the saving depends on which layers receive adapters.
experiment: Read your adapter configuration. List rank, scale, target modules and number of adapted layers. Calculate one layer's trainable parameter count.
question: Does LoRA's smaller parameter count mean its training is guaranteed to match full fine-tuning?
answer: No. It constrains the available update. Data, target modules, rank, optimization and the task determine the result.

title: QLoRA and the frozen quantized base
why: LoRA reduces trainable state, but its frozen base can still be large. Quantizing that base reduces another major memory component.
how: Quantized-base adapter training uses an approximate frozen base alongside trainable adapter values. Computation can use higher-precision reconstructed values. Original QLoRA's NF4 and double-quantization choices are specific methods; an MLX quantized adapter run does not automatically use the same format. Read the actual configuration.
formula: y≈(W_reconstructed+sBA)x. W_reconstructed comes from the packed frozen base. Gradients update selected adapter parameters A and B. Quantized storage does not imply directly applying ordinary floating-point gradient updates to every packed integer code.
example: An illustrative 7B base has ideal 4-bit weight storage of 3.5 GB instead of 14 GB at 16 bits. Adapter parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations still require extra memory; 3.5 GB is not the training budget.
experiment: For your MLX fine-tune, identify the frozen-base quantization mode and the adapter dtype. Compare this with the settings of the model you actually serve.
question: Are all four-bit adapter runs numerically interchangeable with an NF4 QLoRA run?
answer: No. Bit width alone does not identify the codebook, grouping, computation or original base. Match and test the actual artifacts.

title: Why training can run out of memory when inference fits
why: Training must preserve information for backward computation and optimizer updates. A model that generates successfully may still exceed memory during fine-tuning.
how: Weights, trainable gradients, optimizer state and saved activations contribute to memory. Sequence length and microbatch size affect activations. Gradient accumulation combines several smaller microbatches before an update. Checkpointing trades recomputation for fewer saved intermediate values. Neither technique removes every memory cost.
formula: effective examples per update = microbatch size × accumulation steps × worker count, assuming equally sized batches. This is an example count; token-based loss normalization also matters when sequence lengths differ.
example: On one device, microbatch 1 with accumulation 8 collects eight examples before an update. It can lower the peak compared with processing all eight simultaneously, but takes multiple forward/backward passes and keeps accumulated gradients.
experiment: If an existing run fails, reduce sequence length or microbatch size one at a time and record peak memory. Consider accumulation to preserve examples per update; recheck optimization behavior.
question: Does accumulation by eight mean eight full activation graphs must stay in memory at once?
answer: Normally no. Each microbatch can complete backward computation before the next; its gradients accumulate while most of its graph can be released.

title: Learning rate, rank, epochs and overfitting
why: Fine-tuning settings control different mechanisms. Raising all of them after a poor result gives you little explanation for what helped or harmed.
how: Learning rate controls optimizer update scale. Rank controls adapter capacity. An epoch is one pass through the training examples. More passes can improve training fit while worsening unseen behavior. Compare training and validation trends, then inspect application failures.
formula: updates per epoch ≈ ceil(N/E), where N is training examples and E effective examples per optimizer update, assuming batches are handled as stated. Standard LoRA often uses s=alpha/r; rank-stabilized LoRA uses alpha/sqrt(r). Changing rank without considering scaling changes more than capacity.
example: With 800 examples and 8 effective examples per update, one epoch is about 100 updates. Three epochs are about 300. If validation deteriorates after epoch one while training loss improves, more training is not automatically beneficial.
experiment: Write one hypothesis for your next run: learning rate too high, data too narrow or insufficient capacity. Change only the setting that tests it; save the validation outcome and checkpoint identity.
question: If a larger rank performs worse, does that prove LoRA is unsuitable?
answer: No. Scaling, learning rate, data size, target layers and overfitting may explain it. Compare controlled runs.

title: Evaluate adaptation on tasks you actually care about
why: Loss measures token prediction, while your application needs usable outcomes. Evaluation connects training changes to user value.
how: Define a pass condition before examining results. For structured actions, check parsing, required fields, intended action and argument correctness separately. Include ambiguous requests that should produce clarification. Keep your final test set out of training and repeated model selection.
formula: pass rate = passed cases / tested cases. A paired comparison uses the same cases for both models: count newly passed cases and newly failed cases, rather than looking only at the total.
example: An adapter can improve JSON validity from 90/100 to 99/100 while reducing correct dates from 95/100 to 92/100. Better formatting does not erase the new date failures. These counts are an illustration, not your recorded project result.
experiment: Build a small labeled set from your project's actual failure categories. Run base and adapter under matching decoding settings; inspect disagreements before expanding the set.
question: Can a lower validation loss guarantee safer reminder creation?
answer: No. Loss averages token prediction penalties. Application tests must check whether the proposed reminder matches the user's intent and whether approval rules hold.

title: MLX model loading, generation and benchmarking
why: A usable local workflow needs reproducible loading and inference before you add training. This becomes the baseline for every later comparison.
how: MLX LM provides model and tokenizer loading plus text generation. Pin the package version and checkpoint revision, apply the checkpoint's expected chat template, and record generation settings. Separate model download, initial loading, warm-up and steady-state execution when measuring performance.
formula: reproducible run = model revision + tokenizer/template + runtime version + generation settings + input set + device conditions. This is an experiment checklist: leaving one part unknown weakens a before/after comparison.
example: Two runs called 'Qwen 4-bit' can differ in checkpoint, group size, prompt markers and output limit. A faster run with half the output limit does not demonstrate a faster runtime.
experiment: In your installed environment, inspect python -m mlx_lm.generate --help. Use an already downloaded compatible model and one short request. Save the exact invocation and output; consult your installed version's help for supported flags.
question: Should download time be included in a warmed generation-throughput number?
answer: No. Report download and load costs separately, while also reporting cold-start time when that is relevant to the user's experience.

title: Merge, requantize and verify the served artifact
why: The artifact you deploy can differ numerically from the one you evaluated during training. A successful merge command is not proof of unchanged behavior.
how: An adapter may remain separate or be fused into a base weight matrix. If training used a quantized base, reconstructing that base differs from using the original higher-precision checkpoint. Requantizing a merged result adds rounding again. Supported merge paths depend on the runtime and model.
formula: merged W = base W + sBA. In general, Q(W+sBA) ≠ Q(W)+sBA, because quantization Q rounds values. Likewise, reconstructed Q(W) need not equal the original W.
example: A toy base weight 0.30 reconstructed as 0.3333 plus an adapter change 0.02 gives 0.3533. Applying the same change to the original 0.30 gives 0.32 before any later rounding. Neither path can be assumed equivalent.
experiment: Record the exact base, adapter and merge settings. Evaluate the separate-adapter version, merged version and final quantized version on the same cases. Keep the last working artifact available.
question: Does dequantization recover the original high-precision weights exactly?
answer: No. It reconstructs the quantized approximation. Information discarded by rounding is generally lost.

title: An MLX adapter training workflow you can explain
why: The main lesson derives LoRA. This companion turns that mechanism into a reproducible local experiment using your existing MLX experience.
how: First evaluate the base. Prepare training and validation examples in a supported format. Inspect the installed MLX LM training options, select the trainable layers and settings, run a small experiment, then load its adapter with the matching base. An adapter file is not a standalone full language model.
formula: baseline → formatted data → loss and gradients → adapter update → validation → saved adapter + matching base → held-out task test. Each stage has an artifact or measurement you can inspect.
example: For a reminder project, teach a consistent proposal format using varied requests and correct responses. Keep unseen names, dates and clarification cases for evaluation. A formatting gain accompanied by invented dates is not an acceptable overall improvement.
experiment: Inspect python -m mlx_lm.lora --help and the official MLX LM LoRA guide for your version. Write a run sheet containing base revision, data split, template, rank, target layers, learning rate, batch/accumulation, iteration budget and adapter output folder. Run a small local trial only when those choices are clear.
question: What must accompany the adapter when you reproduce an inference result?
answer: The matching base and tokenizer/template, adapter configuration, runtime and decoding settings, plus the same input. The adapter alone does not define the full computation.

title: Distillation and preference learning for smaller models
why: After supervised fine-tuning, a model may still choose poor responses or be too expensive. Preference learning and distillation address different aspects of that problem.
how: Preference data compares a preferred and a dispreferred response to the same prompt. Distillation trains a student using a teacher's outputs or probability distribution. A teacher can be wrong; generated data needs checking. Smaller student size and lower storage precision are separate ways to reduce resources.
formula: For soft-target distillation, L = −sum_i q_i log p_i. q_i is the teacher's target probability for token i and p_i the student's prediction. Minimizing this encourages agreement with the teacher distribution, not automatic agreement with truth.
example: A larger model may draft reminder proposals for training a smaller local model. Validate dates and intent before accepting those examples. Separately, preference pairs can favor asking a necessary clarification over guessing.
experiment: Create five preferred/dispreferred pairs and state a concrete reason for each. Review five teacher-generated examples for factual and format errors before adding any to a dataset.
question: Is a 4-bit version of a model automatically a distilled model?
answer: No. Quantization changes numerical representation; distillation trains a student to imitate a teacher. They can be used together.

title: Audio pipelines: find which model made the mistake
why: A voice application includes several transformations. Fine-tuning the language model cannot reliably repair a fact that was lost before it received the transcript.
how: Audio recognition produces text, the language model interprets it, and the application validates the proposed action. Each stage can introduce errors. The device used for each model depends on its runtime and conversion; do not assume every speech model runs on the Neural Engine.
formula: end-to-end latency ≈ capture/endpointing + transcription + interpretation + validation/action, for sequential stages. Overlapped streaming changes the timing model. End-to-end accuracy cannot generally be found by multiplying unrelated benchmark accuracies.
example: If 'do not remind me today' becomes 'remind me today', a correctly functioning intent model may still propose the wrong action. Compare original audio, transcript and proposal to locate the failure.
experiment: Run the same intent request once from a verified text transcript and once through audio. If only the audio path fails, inspect recognition and endpointing before changing the adapter.
question: Why is word error rate alone insufficient for a reminder application?
answer: One incorrect negation, name or date can change the action, while several harmless filler-word errors may not. Measure downstream intent and argument correctness too.

title: Benchmark local models without misleading yourself
why: Short tests can miss loading costs, thermal changes and variance. A useful report explains the workload and conditions behind each number.
how: Use repeated runs with fixed prompts and output lengths. Report memory, quality, time to first token and later-token speed separately. Record device, power mode, runtime, context and concurrent workload. Compare warm runs fairly and keep cold-start measurements distinct.
formula: mean latency = sum of run times / number of runs. Median is the middle sorted observation; p95 is a high percentile of the measured distribution. A p95 from very few runs is unstable and should not be presented as a production guarantee.
example: A 4-bit model may start faster because fewer bytes are loaded, yet decode at a similar speed because a different cost dominates. A long session may slow as thermal conditions change. Both observations can be real.
experiment: Repeat one representative request at least several times for each artifact. Save individual observations, not only their average. Explain the sample size and avoid claiming a precise tail latency from a tiny sample.
question: Can an isolated best-case timing defend a latency guarantee?
answer: No. It demonstrates one run under one condition. Guarantees need representative workloads, enough observations and clearly defined boundaries.

title: Choose a model by its quality–memory–latency tradeoff
why: The smallest artifact is not always the best application choice, and the largest model is not always worth its cost. Selection needs explicit constraints.
how: Set minimum task quality and maximum memory/latency budgets, then compare candidates that meet them. A larger 4-bit model and a smaller 8-bit model differ in both learned capacity and precision. Changing both is a product comparison, not an isolated quantization experiment.
formula: candidate is feasible when quality ≥ required quality, peak memory ≤ memory budget, and measured latency ≤ latency budget. These conditions express your requirements; their thresholds must come from the application.
example: Suppose one candidate uses 3 GB with 92/100 task passes and another uses 5 GB with 97/100. If your device budget is 4 GB, the second cannot be selected unchanged. If the five failures are critical, the first may also be unacceptable.
experiment: Build a decision table for your actual MLX artifacts. Explain one rejected candidate and one unresolved measurement. Consider routing or a simpler non-model solution when no candidate meets requirements.
question: Can you infer whether a 7B 4-bit model beats a 3B 8-bit model just from their names?
answer: No. Architecture, training and task fit differ. Evaluate both under your application's constraints.

title: Debug local inference one stage at a time
why: A changed output has many possible causes. A controlled diagnosis prevents unnecessary retraining and helps you learn what each component does.
how: Start from a saved working input and artifact. Check input formatting, tokenizer and stop settings, then base/adapter identity, conversion settings and runtime. For slowdowns, separate loading, prompt length, decode, memory pressure and thermal conditions. Change one suspected cause at a time.
formula: observed difference = new run − baseline run, with all unrelated conditions held fixed where possible. This is an experimental comparison, not a claim that all effects add linearly.
example: If only the merged 4-bit version fails a date test while the separate adapter passes, inspect merge and conversion before collecting more training data. If both fail on the same audio transcript, check the transcript and task examples.
experiment: Write a failure report with one minimal input, expected result, actual result, artifact versions and the first experiment that distinguishes two plausible causes.
question: What does 'try a lower learning rate' fail to explain when only inference is slow?
answer: Learning rate controls training updates. Inference latency is more directly connected to workload, model size, kernels, memory and hardware conditions.

title: Capstone: defend your own local model release
why: The goal is to explain the model you have used, not merely recognize terms. A small reproducible comparison makes the concepts concrete.
how: Choose an existing project and follow one input through formatting, model computation, token selection and application validation. Compare a baseline with one adaptation or precision change. Preserve the artifact identities and test results needed to reproduce the conclusion.
formula: release evidence = reproducible configuration + held-out task results + resource measurements + failure analysis + rollback artifact. This is a reasoning checklist, not a numerical quality score.
example: For a NoteEchoes-style project, explain why you selected a particular base and 4-bit or 8-bit representation, what the adapter learned, what stays outside the model, which cases still fail and what memory/latency you actually measured.
experiment: Produce a one-page report with your model/config inventory, three worked calculations from this track, a controlled comparison table, two inspected failures and your selection decision. Mark missing evidence explicitly. No new download or expensive training run is required to begin.
question: What distinguishes 'I used MLX and QLoRA' from understanding the system?
answer: You can explain what the runtime executes, what is frozen or trained, how numbers are represented, why memory changes, how you verified quality and where your evidence stops.
